items.quote: CHAP. I. Of the True Physick.
items.note: The chapter is headed and numbered as treating one thing, the true Physick.

items.quote: THE true Physick whereof by the Devine assistance I intend here to treat
items.note: The author announces the subject he will treat, in his own voice.

items.quote: is the mear gift of the most high God; it is not to be sought for or learned from the Heathens, but from God alone
items.note: The author holds that true Physick is God's gift and is learned from God, not from the Heathens.

items.quote: See Paracels. his Labyrinth of Physitians.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: A margin note beside the claim that Physick is learned from God alone names a writing of Paracelsus, the Labyrinth of Physitians.

items.quote: Wisdome therefore is not to be got from the Creatures, but from God, who being the first inventer of all Secrets
items.note: Wisdom comes from God as the first inventor of all secrets, not from creatures.

items.quote: no mortall Master or dead letter can ever teach it so well as he, who is the perfect Artist of all things
items.note: Neither a human master nor written letter teaches this knowledge as well as God.

items.quote: All learn of the first by retrogression or going backward
items.note: The text glosses its own word retrogression as going backward: learning goes back to the first, and the first learned of God.

items.quote: A Physitian should be born out of the Light of Grace and Nature of the inward and invisible Man, the internall Angell, the Light of Nature
items.note: The physician arises from an inward light, which the text calls the internal Angel and the Light of Nature; it teaches like a doctor, compared to the Spirit teaching the Apostles.

items.quote: upon Nature, upon which God hath written with his own sacred finger in sublunary things, but especially in perfect Mettalls
items.note: Nature is spoken of as a writing by God's finger, most of all in perfect metals; the text marks metals as the chief place where this writing is found.

items.quote: God therefore is the true Foundation thereof.
items.note: The author names God as the true foundation of Physick.

items.quote: The Master teacheth that Scholler in vaine whose Nativity is not disposed to that Art by the Sears.
items.note: A margin note holds that teaching is vain for a scholar whose nativity is not disposed to the art; the last word is printed Sears.

items.quote: Wherefore Physick is nothing else but the created and incarnate Mercy of our Heavenly Father
items.note: The text says what Physick is: God's mercy made created and incarnate, given to the sick so that God is glorified.

items.quote: whereof University books are not the Foundation, but the invisible mercy of God and his speciall gift
items.note: The margin note denies that university books are the foundation of Physick.

items.quote: This Physicall essence in Phisick is called Gold.
items.note: The margin note gives a name to the physical essence in Physick: it is called Gold. The word is used for something other than the plain metal here.

items.quote: Physick is written in the book of Nature
items.note: Physick is spoken of as written in a book of Nature, in Heaven and Earth, to be read by Chyromancy and phisiognomy through God's illumination.

items.quote: may there be read & found out by Chyromancy and phisiognomy, through the miraculous illumination of God
items.note: The note names how the book of Nature is read: Chyromancy and phisiognomy, with God's illumination.

items.quote: this Medicine, as naturall Mummy and kernell of Nature, is contained in the vitall Sulphur, as in the treasure of Nature
items.what: this Medicine, as naturall Mummy and kernell of Nature
items.note: The Medicine is named natural Mummy and kernel of Nature, and placed in the vital Sulphur.

items.quote: is founded in the Balsam of Vegetables, Mineralls and Animalls, from which every action in Nature hath its beginning
items.note: The Medicine is founded in a Balsam present in all three kingdoms, the beginning of every action in nature.

items.quote: By its onely power all diseases are cured
items.note: The author claims this Medicine alone cures all diseases, on the condition that follows.

items.quote: if (as shall be shewed anon) it be rightly prepared
items.note: The text promises to show later how the Medicine is rightly prepared.

items.quote: it be rightly prepared, and separated from all impurity, and in a due order conveniently administred by a Godly skilfull Phisitian
items.note: Steps named: preparation, separation from all impurity, and ordered administration by a godly skilful physician. How each is done is not given here.

items.quote: The Foundation of this Physick is according to the agreement of the lesser World Man with the greater and externall world
items.note: The foundation of Physick is named as the agreement of the lesser world, Man, with the greater world.

items.quote: Philosophy teatheth the force and properties of Earth and Wate
items.note: The text assigns Philosophy to Earth and Water and Astronomy to the Firmament and Air; it uses both words in this narrowed sense.

items.quote: Phylosophy and Astronomy make up an internall and perfect Phylosopher, not onely in the great World, but also in the lesser
items.note: Both together make the perfect philosopher, in the great and the lesser world.

items.quote: duly compare the Anotomy of the World with the Anotomy of Man
items.note: The method required: compare the great world as parent with man as son, anatomy against anatomy.

items.quote: The outward World is a speculative Anotomy, wherein we may see, as in a glasse, the lesser World Man
items.note: The outward world is defined as a speculative anatomy, a glass in which man is seen.

items.quote: but in all their powers and vertues; as is the great world, so is the lesser, in essence and internall form they are altogether one and the same thing
items.note: World and man differ in outward form but are one in powers, virtues, essence and internal form.

items.quote: What the Light of Nature is.
items.note: A margin note heads the passage as saying what the Light of Nature is.

items.quote: the Light of Nature, which is nothing else but a divine Analogy of this visible world with the body of man
items.note: The text defines the Light of Nature as a divine analogy between the visible world and man's body.

items.quote: Without the knowledge of Light of Nature or the great world no Physitian can have an exact knowledge of diseases in Man.
items.note: Knowledge of the great world is required to know diseases in man.

items.quote: whatsoever lyeth hid and unseen in Man, is made manifest in the visible Anotomy of the whole Universe
items.note: What is hidden in man is made visible in the universe; the hidden here is the invisible nature of man, read through the world.

items.quote: for the Microcosmicall Nature in Man is invisible and incomprehensible
items.note: The nature of man as microcosm cannot be seen or grasped in man himself.

items.quote: The great World is a speculation and glasse of the little World Man.
items.note: The margin note restates the great world as a glass of man.

items.quote: Heaven and Earth are Man's Parents, out of which Man last of all was created
items.note: Man is made last, out of Heaven and Earth as his parents.

items.quote: and can Anotomize them, hath attained the true knowledge of their child Man
items.note: Whoever can anatomize the parents, Heaven and Earth, knows man, in whom all things of the universe meet as in a centre.

items.quote: Man is the End of Phylosophy and Astronomy.
items.note: Man is named the end of both sciences.

items.quote: The externall world is the figure of Man, and Man is an hidden world, because visible things in him are invisible
items.note: The text calls man a hidden world and gives its reason: what is visible in him is invisible.

items.quote: when they are made visible then they are diseases, not health
items.note: The invisible things in man, once made visible, are diseases.

items.quote: Man may Microcosmically be known visibly and invisibly or magically
items.note: Knowing man invisibly is equated with knowing him magically; the text sets magically beside invisibly.

items.quote: the Nature, as well of the Macrocosme as the Microcosme, is its own medicine, disease, and Physitian
items.note: Nature in both worlds is at once medicine, disease and physician.

items.quote: Nature, not man, maketh a Physitian.
items.note: The physician is made by Nature, not by man.

items.quote: the Matter of Man is the Extract of the four Elements
items.note: Man's matter is called the extract of the four elements; hence he needs all elements and their fruits.

items.quote: God created the Elements for their fruits sake, that they might sustaine and preserve Man with food and Physick.
items.note: The elements exist for their fruits, which feed and heal man.

items.quote: The knowledge of the 4 Elements doe shew every disease in man and its cure.
items.note: Knowing the four elements shows every disease and its cure.

items.quote: in the foure Elements there is but one Anatomy essence and matter, all the differenc being onely in the Form
items.note: The four elements share one essence and matter and differ only in form.

items.quote: The knowledge of Physick in the outward world is to be fetched from the Limbovn, and depends upon the knowledg of Man.
items.note: The margin note sends knowledge of Physick to the Limbovn, a word the lines given do not explain.

items.quote: Lastly Airy Fre, Airy Water, Airy Earth.
items.what: Fire, Aire, Earthy Water ... Caelestiall Earth ... Terrene, Fiery, Airy Water ... Airy Fre, Airy Water, Airy Earth
items.note: A fourfold series of mixed elements is set out in four steps (Thus, Againe, Likewise, Lastly); as printed the series is irregular and does not give four full sets.

items.quote: There are also four kinds of Mercury, and four sorts of Mettalls, a fourfold Snow, four sorts of Ametheists and precious stones
items.what: four kinds of Mercury, four sorts of Mettalls, a fourfold Snow, four sorts of Ametheists
items.note: Things are counted as fourfold, one for each element.

items.quote: There are Foure of every thing, one in the Firmament or Heavenly Element
items.note: Every thing exists four times, in Firmament, Air, Water and Earth.

items.quote: Every Element perfecteth its power and operation in all the four Elements.
items.note: Each element works in all four.

items.quote: So there is a fourfold Man; For God is far more wonderfull in his invisible works then in his visible.
items.note: Man too is named fourfold; the invisible works are placed above the visible.

items.quote: Paracelsus faith, that to avoyd an Emptiness in all the four Elements, he created living creatures
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The account of the elemental inhabitants is given as what Paracelsus says (the verb is printed faith). The following lists (CH1.8 to CH1.11) appear to continue it; the text does not mark where his words end.

items.quote: inanimate, that is to say, without an Intellectuall Soule
items.note: The text glosses inanimate as without an intellectual soul; these beings differ from men made in God's image.

items.quote: To the Water there belong Nimphs, Undens, Melosyns, whose Monsters or bastards are the Syrens that swim upon the water.
items.note: The inhabitants of Water and their monsters are named.

items.quote: To the Earth doe belong Gnoms, Lemurs, Sylphs, Montans, Zonnets, whose Monsters are the Pigmyes.
items.what: Gnoms, Lemurs, Sylphs, Montans, Zonnets; Pigmyes
items.note: The inhabitants of Earth and their monsters are named; Sylphs stand here under Earth.

items.quote: Satyrs, whose Monsters are the Gyants
items.note: The inhabitants of the Air and their monsters; one name has an illegible letter.

items.quote: To the Fire or the Firmament doe belong the Vulcanals, Pennats, Salamanders, Superi, whose Monsters are Zundell
items.note: The inhabitants of Fire or the Firmament and their monsters are named.

items.quote: Flagae which Theophrastus in his works affirmeth are in many thousands of severall forts incorporated to the Soul of the World
items.name: Theophrastus
items.note: The Flagae are reported as what Theophrastus affirms in his works.

items.quote: Thus also there is a fourfold Medicine
items.note: Medicine is named fourfold, matching the fourfold elements and man.

items.quote: the fiery, airy, watry, earthy Heart of the Macrocosm in all things agreeable to the Heart of the Microcosm Man
items.note: Each member of man answers to a fourfold member of the great world, the heart given as example.

items.quote: every malady and medicine is of the same Physiognomy, Chyromancy and Anotomy; He that knows not this Fundamentall cannot be a good Phisitian
items.note: The correspondence is named a Fundamentall without which no one is a good physician.

items.quote: we find out of ancient Records that Astrologers and Chymiologers were very near of kin
items.note: On the authority of ancient records, unnamed, astrologers and chymiologers are kin.

items.quote: the Astrology of superiour things hath to doe with the Chymiology of things inferiour
items.note: Astrology governs the superior things and Chymiology the inferior; each has its own heaven, sun, moon, planets and stars.

items.quote: these can easily and truly unfold all Phylosophicall difficulties that have been wrapt up in aenigmaticall obscurity
items.note: Philosophical matters are said to be wrapped in enigmatic obscurity; only chymists who by divine grace have attained the Mind can unfold them.

items.quote: Those Chymists who by the assistance of divine Grace have attained the Mind
items.note: The Mind is used as the name of something attained, a condition for unfolding the enigmas; the lines given do not say what it is.

items.quote: they need not travell to India or America to get the knowledge of Phylosophy
items.note: Such chymists need not travel far for philosophy.

items.quote: the invisible Astra's of the other Elements should be represented by a visible appearance in the supream Element
items.note: The invisible Astra of the lower elements are shown visibly in the highest element, the inferior nature having in-bred Astra.

items.quote: Thus as P. Severinus the Dane doth learnedly observe
items.name: P. Severinus the Dane
items.note: The account of seasonal constellations within Earth, Water and Air is given as Severinus's observation.

items.quote: the (Sidus) constellation of Summer, Winter, Spring Autumn, are contained in the Earth, Water, Aire
items.note: The text sets the word Sidus beside constellation as its gloss.

items.quote: to which onely many of the common Phylosophers by a great mistake have ascribed all Astronomy
items.name: common Phylosophers
items.note: A view of the common philosophers is reported in order to reject it: that all astronomy belongs to the Firmament's Astra only.

items.quote: In his Idaea of Phylosophical Phifick.
items.name: Idaea of Phylosophical Phifick
items.note: The margin note names the writing of Severinus the passage draws on.

items.quote: their paine many times makes them Prophets and Astrologers against their will
items.note: Gout sufferers foresee changes of season; the note uses this to show inner elements sense outer ones.

items.quote: As Reason rules the outward Astra's, so Physick rules the inward.
items.note: Reason rules the outer Astra, Physick the inner.

items.quote: The Astrum of Man and Heaven is but one.
items.note: Man's Astrum and Heaven's are one.

items.quote: There is a twofold Heaven; Externall, as all the bodies of the Astra's in the Heaven of the Firmament
items.note: Heaven is divided into external and internal.

items.quote: Internall, which is the Astrum or invisible and insensible body in all the Stars of Heaven
items.note: The internal Heaven is defined as the Astrum, the invisible and insensible body in the stars.

items.quote: That invisible and insensible body of the Astra's is the Spirit of the World, or Nature, as Paracelsus calls it, the Hylech
items.note: The invisible body of the Astra is named Spirit of the World, Nature, and, after Paracelsus, Hylech.

items.quote: as Paracelsus calls it, the Hylech
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The name Hylech is given as Paracelsus's word.

items.quote: the internall Heaven of Man, which is the Olimpick spirit
items.note: Man's internal Heaven is named the Olimpick spirit; it contains all the Astra as the Hylech does in the great world.

items.quote: the invisible Man is not onely all the Astra's, but is altogether one and the same thing with the Spirit of the world, as whitenesse is with snow
items.note: The invisible man is identical with the Spirit of the World.

items.quote: proceed from incorporall, spirituall (things) out of the Astra's
items.note: Visible bodies come from invisible spiritual things, out of the Astra, and remain in them.

items.quote: are indued with a syderiall spirit, which is called Heaven or the Astrum, the secret Forger, from which every Formation, Figure and Colour of things proceedeth
items.note: All things, stones and metals too, have a sidereal spirit, called Heaven, Astrum, the secret Forger; form, figure and colour come from it.

items.quote: The Sun of the Microcosm (which Paracelsus calls the Ens or Being of the seed and virtue or power)
items.note: Man's own Astrum is named the Sun of the Microcosm, and after Paracelsus the Ens, glossed as Being.

items.quote: which Paracelsus calls the Ens or Being of the seed and virtue or power
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The term Ens is given as Paracelsus's.

items.quote: as iron in the imagination of the Smith
items.note: The margin note compares the formation of things in the Astra to iron in a smith's imagination.

items.quote: Hence also Nativities are to be cast
items.note: The note draws from the inner Astrum that nativities are to be cast.

items.quote: in Paramiro de eme Astro
items.name: Paramiro
items.note: The note refers to a writing of Paracelsus, Paramiro; the title is partly illegible.

items.quote: it is not meant of the visible coales of Heaven, nor of the invisible body of the Astra's in the Firmament, but of every things own proper Astrum
items.note: The text says what its own phrase means: form from the Astra means each thing's own Astrum, not the stars above.

items.quote: the superior doth not power forth its vertues & hidden secrets into the inferiour spectificate Firmament
items.note: The superior heaven does not pour its virtues into lower things.

items.quote: the superior doth not power forth its vertues & hidden secrets into the inferiour spectificate Firmament
items.note: Here the upper heaven pours no virtues into lower things; CH1.12 calls the celestial Astronomy the parent and mistress of the inferior. Parenthood may not mean infusion; the text does not say.

items.quote: as the false Philosophers thinke that the stars of the Firmament do infuse virtue into herbs and trees
items.name: false Philosophers
items.note: A view reported in order to reject it.

items.quote: every growing and living thing carry its proper heaven and Astrum with it selfe, and in it selfe
items.note: Each thing carries its own heaven within.

items.quote: the superiour stars in their course through the Zodiak excite and stir up the growth of inferiour things
items.note: The upper stars only stir growth and provide dew, rain and seasons; they do not infuse smell, colour or form.

items.quote: the externall stars do neither incline nor necessitate Man
items.note: External stars neither incline nor compel man.

items.quote: but Man rather inclines the Stars, and by his Magicall imagination infecteth them, and causeth those deadly impressions
items.note: Man acts on the stars through his magical imagination and causes harmful impressions.

items.quote: Man governeth the Stars and not the Stars him.
items.note: The margin note restates the claim.

items.quote: we receive not our conditions, properties, and manners from the Ascendant, nor from the Constellation of the Planets, but from the hand of God through the breathing in of the breath of life
items.note: Man's conditions come from God's breath of life, not the Ascendant or planets.

items.quote: the externall stars do neither incline nor necessitate Man
items.note: Here the stars neither incline man, and his conditions do not come from the Ascendant; N037 speaks of a scholar's Nativity disposed to an art, and N047 says nativities are to be cast. The notes may mean the inner Astrum, which the lines given do not settle.

items.quote: Read the eight Psalme.
items.name: the eight Psalme
items.note: The margin note sends the reader to the eighth Psalm beside the breath of life and man's rule over the stars.

items.quote: So that Mans Reason ought to rule the externall Stars.
items.note: Man's reason should rule the outer stars.

items.quote: For if we that are the children of Adam did not provoke our Father with our sins we should alwayes find him meek and gentle towards us
items.note: Harm is laid to sin provoking God, not to the stars.

items.quote: see Paracels. in Paramiro lib. 2. de origine morbor. cap. 7.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: The text refers to a named book and chapter of Paracelsus's Paramiro.

items.quote: Vid. Paracels.
items.name: Paracels.
items.note: A margin note names Paracelsus beside the passage.

items.quote: So the course of the Firmament and Stars in Man is free, with their Constellations, and not at all governed by the outward Firmament
items.note: Man's inner firmament runs free of the outer, as the outer runs free of all.

items.quote: which course is not finished materially, but in the spirits of bodies
items.note: The inner course runs in the spirits of bodies, not materially.

items.quote: as the Aire or Sun cannot set an apple or pear upon the tree
items.note: Fruit grows from its own inner Astrum from centre to circumference; the outer heaven infuses no virtue.

items.quote: doe indeavour and bend to one generall Good as Citizens of the same Anotmy
items.note: The fruits of the Astra, of all four kinds, serve one common good and help one another.

items.quote: This visible and invisible fellowship of Nature is that golden chaine so much commended, this is the marriage of heaven and riches, these are Plato's rings
items.note: The text says what the golden chain, the marriage of heaven and riches, and Plato's rings mean: the fellowship of Nature.

items.quote: Plato's Rings and Homers Chaines are nothing but a Divine Series and Order serving Providence, a graduall and concatenate Sympathy of things
items.note: The margin note defines Plato's rings and Homer's chains as a graded sympathy of things.

items.quote: this is that dark and close Phylosophy so hard to be known in the most inward and secret parts of Natare
items.note: This fellowship is called a dark and close philosophy, hard to know, in the secret parts of Nature.

items.quote: have travelled to the Brachmans and Gymnosophists in the Indies, and to Hermes his Pillars in Aegypt
items.note: The author says Democritus, Pythagoras, Plato, Apollonius and others travelled to seek this philosophy; CH1.12 says the chymists who attain the Mind need not travel.

items.quote: which by the Light of Nature that singular inspiration of God they also obtained
items.note: The Light of Nature is called a singular inspiration of God; CH1.5 called it a divine analogy.

items.quote: there are THREE Principles of all things which are found in every compound body
items.note: The three Principles are announced, the word THREE in capitals.

items.quote: No body compos'd by Nature can by any dissolving skill be parted into more or lesse then Three, viz. Into Mercury or liquor, Sulphur or Oyle, and Salt
items.note: Every natural body resolves into exactly three: Mercury or liquor, Sulphur or oil, Salt.

items.quote: the Holy Triunity when it spake that Triune word FIAT created all things Triune, as in a Spagiricall resolution is plainly to be seen
items.note: The threefold make-up of things is traced to the Triune word FIAT and said to be seen in Spagiric resolution.

items.quote: i. e. A seperation of purity from impurity, or truth from falshood.
items.note: The margin note glosses Spagiricall resolution as separating pure from impure, true from false.

items.quote: By the word FIAT (or Let there be) God produced the first matter, which is threefold in respect of the three Principles contained in the first
items.note: FIAT is glossed Let there be; the first matter is threefold, later separated into four bodies or Elements.

items.quote: just as if a skillfull Artist should out of lead make red lead, white lead, Glasse, and the Spirit of lead
items.note: An artist's working of lead into four products is given as likeness of the first matter separated into four Elements.

items.quote: the world with all created bodies in it is nothing else but a fume or smoak coagulated or curded together of the three substances, Sulphur Salt, Mercury
items.note: The world is defined as a coagulated smoke of the three substances.

items.quote: The Spagyricks can make this plaine by visible experience and uncontroulable certainty.
items.note: The Spagyricks are said to show the three by experience.

items.quote: these two are consumed by the fire; The third, viz. the Salt is unctuous, very little, thin and lasting, and remains in the ashes
items.note: Burning green wood: the watery moisture like Mercury and the oily like brimstone are consumed; the Salt remains in the ashes.

items.quote: The Salt by coagulation gives Solidity, Colour and Tast to all bodies
items.note: The office of Salt.

items.quote: The Sulphur by a pleasant mixture tempereth the coagulation of the Salt, and gives the Body Substance and Transmutation
items.note: The office of Sulphur.

items.quote: Mercury, which like the Elixir giveth the vertues
items.note: Mercury is likened to the Elixir; it gives virtues, operations and secrets and feeds the other two.

items.quote: When the Salt or Mummy is spent things br
items.note: The margin note sets Salt and Mummy as one (Salt or Mummy); CH1.3 called the Medicine natural Mummy contained in the vital Sulphur.

items.quote: These three Principles which are in all bodies are altogether distinct in use and properties
items.note: The three are distinct in use though they appear to sense as one substance.

items.quote: Some Theophrastaeans, who have more narrowly and exactly searched out the causes of hidden things doe add a Fourth
items.name: Some Theophrastaeans
items.note: A fourth principle, the Spirit, is reported as added by some Theophrastaeans, not as the author's own.

items.quote: which though it may be got out of Mineralls and Vegetables, yet in Animalls by reason of its subtility
items.note: The Spirit can be got from minerals and vegetables but not separated in animals because of its subtlety.

items.quote: The Spirit of God upon the face of the waters.
items.note: The margin note sets the Spirit of God beside the fourth principle called the Spirit.

items.quote: thus Sulphur or brimstone may answer to Fire, Salt to the earth, Mercury to Water, Spirit to Aire
items.note: The four principles are matched to the four elements.

items.quote: we shall add a few things concerning them out of that short Treatise of Severinus
items.name: Severinus
items.note: What follows on the elements is taken from a treatise of Severinus; the text does not mark where his matter ends.

items.quote: The true and purely spirituall Elements are the keepers, nurses, places, Mines, wombs and receptacles of the whole Creation
items.note: The true Elements are defined as places and receptacles of creation, and the life and act of beings.

items.quote: to the Seeds that they may produce out of themselves the things that were secretly treasured up in them
items.note: Things lie secretly stored in the seeds, to be brought out by them.

items.quote: These (places) are divided into two Globes, viz. the superiour Fire, or the Firmament, and Aire, much like the shell and white of an egge
items.note: The Elements are grouped into two globes, upper and lower, likened to an egg.

items.quote: and of the Spirit moving upon the face of the Waters, did plant the Light and Seminall causes of all things
items.note: God planted the light and seminal causes in the four empty natures by the Word and the Spirit.

items.quote: Gen. 1.
items.name: Gen.
items.note: The margin note names Genesis 1 beside the account of creation.

items.quote: shall ever be supplyed by an incomprehensible Magick out of the Eternall Treasures of Divine Wisdome
items.note: Ongoing supply of the seminal causes is called an incomprehensible Magick.

items.quote: The Seeds and Astra's, those bonds of things, lay hid in the invisible Treasures of the Elements from the beginning of the Creation, as in a great deep
items.note: The seeds and Astra lie hidden in the elements and spring up in their appointed times.

items.quote: The knowledge of the Elements cannot be attained unto without these Seeds
items.note: The elements are known only through the seeds.

items.quote: as the seeds are to the Elements, so the Principles of bodies are to them
items.note: The Principles stand to the seeds as the seeds to the Elements, joined by an indissoluble tie.

items.quote: receive strength of Generation and Multiplication from the authority of His Word, whose command all things obey
items.note: Seeds and Principles get power to generate and multiply from God's Word.

items.quote: Hippocr. in lib. de Antiqua medic.
items.name: Hippocr.
items.note: The margin note names a writing of Hippocrates beside the passage.

items.quote: so neither can the Elements and Principles of bodies, the lawes of Nature scarce ever suffered them perfectly to be seperated by any industry of Art
items.note: Elements and Principles can scarcely ever be perfectly separated by art.

items.quote: the lawes of Nature scarce ever suffered them perfectly to be seperated by any industry of Art
items.note: Here art scarcely ever separates Elements and Principles; CH1.19 says Spagiric resolution plainly shows the three and the Spagyricks make it plain by experience. The two may speak of different separations; the text given does not settle it. CH1.23 may still be Severinus's matter.

items.quote: All things proceeds from their powers.
items.note: A margin note: all things come from their powers.
